It leaves the balloon's upper-right edge at about 45 degrees, pointing up and to the right (base near x 788, y 1935; tip near x 863, y 1862 in the 1838-wide original). Followed further, that line runs to Ibrahim's mouth and beard (about x 1000, y 1710). Nagoji's head (mouth about x 740, y 1645) is up and to the LEFT of the tip, the opposite way. The tip does stop on the edge of Nagoji's rolled right sleeve at the elbow, but only because his arm lies between the balloon and Ibrahim. A tail meant for Nagoji would point up toward his head, not sideways past his elbow toward the other man's face. Other cues also give the line to Ibrahim. Nagoji's mouth is closed and he faces forward. Ibrahim's mouth is open, he leans in and gestures toward Nagoji, and the second balloon's tail clearly lands on him. The words themselves ("Do not look for the sardar ... You will see") are advice to a newcomer and flow straight into Ibrahim's second line, so the script's attribution comes through. At print size this is not a wrong speaker tail. The one small polish point left: lengthening the tail about 60 to 100 px so its tip clears Nagoji's sleeve and ends in the gap toward Ibrahim's face would remove the slight overlap.

refuted.description: Wrong speaker tail on Padmini's verbatim line 'I own this land. Why should I not?'. The tail points at Nagoji, so a must-keep line is attributed to him.
refuted.reason:
The art does not show a tail that ends on Nagoji. I zoomed into page 9, panel 9.4 at 4x and 6x. The tail of "I own this land. Why should I not?" leaves the balloon on the left, crosses over Nagoji's forearm and sash, and runs past his right sleeve. Its tip stops on the empty flagstones between the two figures, about 11 px beyond his sleeve (near x≈650, y≈2391 in the 1838 px render), and points right and slightly upward at Padmini's shoulder and face. So the tail points past him toward her. It does not point at him.

The order of the balloons makes the speakers clear too. The upper balloon, "You speak freely, Amma.", points down at Nagoji's tilted-back, laughing head, which is correct. The lower balloon answers "Amma" with a landowner's line that only Padmini can say. That matches the script (lines 279 to 281: NAGOJI, then PADMINI). At print size (about one third of the render), a reader takes the first line as his and the reply as hers.

What is left is a small lettering issue. The tail is drawn across Nagoji's body, and its tip ends closer to him (about 1 mm at print) than to Padmini (about 2.5 mm). A letterer could lengthen it to reach her or route it around his arm. That is polish, not a wrong speaker attribution, so the major finding is refuted.

refuted.description: The crop and caption hide the lead rider, so the beat is lost. Nagoji is meant to lead the returning column with the riders behind him watching his back. Here he is shoved to the right edge, his turban is cut by the top border and the second caption covers his torso, and every rider faces the camera beside him instead of watching him from behind.
refuted.reason: I zoomed into page 1, panel 1.4 and the art doesn't support the main claim. (1) Nagoji is not reduced to a sliver. His whole face shows from brow to chin, with the moustache, earring and rust-red turban. Below the caption you can see his red sash, his hand on the reins and the plain grey gelding, so he's easy to identify at print size. He sits at about two-thirds of the panel width, not at the edge. (2) The shot looks at the column head-on, so the rider nearest the camera is the one in front. Nagoji is the largest and nearest figure, and the riders on the left are drawn smaller, which puts them behind him. That fits the script's "Nagoji at the head... not turning around", since he faces straight ahead. (3) The riders are not all looking at the camera. The two left-hand riders in white turbans have their eyes turned toward Nagoji (screen right), so they are watching him, which is the beat. Only the rider in the middle distance looks at the camera. The other details in the script are there too: a saddled horse with no rider in the middle, bandaged forearms on the right-hand riders, no blood, and a dusk village road. The beat comes through. Two small polish issues are real: the top of the turban is cut by the top border, and the second caption sits over his right shoulder and chest, though not his face. Moving that caption to the right edge, over the background riders, would clear it. Neither problem hides the action or the beat, so they don't count as major.
